runTimeout.description: Maximum runtime (seconds) of an episode (not necessarily DONE).

savePrompt.description: If true, the LLM prompt produced by the harness is included as a 'prompt' field on the action returned by core_harness, which causes it to be persisted in the episode replay. Defaults to false to keep replays small.

seed.description: Integer currently only used for selecting starting position.

strictMode.description: If true, agents must return only {'submission': int} (no extra fields like 'thoughts'), and per-agent TIMEOUT/ERROR/INVALID counts as a loss for the offending agent only — other agents win. If false (default), any agent error halts and voids the entire episode, matching the lenient research-mode behavior.

useImage.description: If true, indicates the observation is intended to be rendered as an image. Note that currently the agent harness is responsible for the actual rendering; no image is passed in the observation.

useOpenings.description: Whether to start from a position in an opening book.

currentPlayer.description: ID of player whose turn it is.

legalActionStrings.description: List of OpenSpiel legal action strings. Only included if includeLegalActions is true.

legalActions.description: List of OpenSpiel legal action integers. Only included if includeLegalActions is true.

openSpielGameName.description: Short name of the OpenSpiel game.

playerId.description: ID of the agent receiving this observation.

serializedGameAndState.description: Enables reconstructing the Game and State objects.

remainingOverageTime.description: Total remaining banked time (seconds) that can be used in excess of per-step actTimeouts -- agent is disqualified with TIMEOUT status when this drops below 0.

action.thoughts:
The current board is almost entirely empty, with activity isolated to the central column (column 3): an x at row 5 (bottom) and an o directly above it at row 4. No player has three consecutive pieces in any direction, so there are no immediate threats to block and no forced wins available on this turn.  

In Connect X (standard Connect 4 rules), the center column is the highest-value area for long-term control because it participates in the most potential winning lines (vertical, horizontal, and both diagonals). By responding in column 3, I place an x at row 3. This has two strategic benefits:  
- It maintains first-player control of the center.  
- It inserts an x between the existing pieces in column 3, preventing the opponent from immediately forming two consecutive o's vertically in the center (which would occur if I played elsewhere and the opponent responded in column 3).  

Alternative moves in columns 2 or 4 are reasonable for building adjacent bottom-row or diagonal structures, but they surrender central control at a stage where the center is still fully contestable. Playing in column 3 is the positionally strongest choice and aligns with optimal opening theory for this game.  

Final Answer: 3

action.thoughts:
The board is almost entirely empty, with all 4 existing pieces confined to column 3 (0-based). From the bottom row upward, column 3 contains x, o, x, o. This means the two x pieces in that column are vertically separated by an o and do not form a connected group of any length.

Any legal move in an empty column (0, 1, 2, 4, 5, or 6) drops the new x piece to the bottom row (row 0). The only moves that immediately create a connected pair are column 2 (adjacent left of the bottom-row x) or column 4 (adjacent right). This produces two horizontally adjacent x pieces at the bottom of the board, which can be extended into longer lines later. All other bottom-row placements leave the new x completely isolated from both existing x pieces.

Placing the new x in column 3 (at row 4) is inferior: the new piece sits directly above an o and is separated from both existing x pieces by o's, forming three completely disconnected x pieces. No horizontal, vertical, or diagonal connection is created, and the alternating pattern in column 3 already prevents any future vertical 4-in-a-row in that column regardless of further play there.

Columns 2 and 4 are perfectly symmetric given the current board, so either is optimal. Column 2 is selected.

Final Answer: 2

The current board has x pieces at (row 5, col 2), (row 5, col 3), and (row 3, col 3), with o pieces clustered in column 3. No player has 4-in-a-row yet, and neither has an immediate winning move available. However, the two x pieces on the bottom row (row 5) are adjacent.  

Dropping an x into column 4 causes it to land at (row 5, col 4). This creates three consecutive x pieces horizontally across columns 2-4 on row 5. The open ends of this line now create two independent winning threats:  
- A follow-up drop in column 1 would complete four x in a row (columns 1-4).  
- A follow-up drop in column 5 would complete four x in a row (columns 2-5).  

After this move, the opponent can block at most one of those two columns on their turn. On the subsequent turn, the second winning column remains open, allowing an immediate win. No other single move creates a comparable forced win (or faster win). Moves such as column 1 create an analogous fork but column 4 is selected here. The opponent has no counter-threats that can be realized before this line is completed.  

Final Answer: 4
